title: Basic Questions (Wer, Wie, Woher)
whyItMatters: An introduction becomes a conversation only when you can ask for information as well as give it. A small group of question words lets you learn someone's name, identity, origin, residence, and languages.

mentalModel.title: Match one question word to one information type
mentalModel.content: Use 'wer' for a person or identity, 'wie' for a name or manner, 'woher' for origin, and 'wo' for location or residence.

mentalModel.title: Question word, verb, subject
mentalModel.content: Build the core question in three steps: question word first, conjugated verb second, subject third: 'Woher kommen Sie?'

mentalModel.title: Ask, answer, return
mentalModel.content: A natural first meeting alternates between one question and one short answer. After answering, return the question with 'Und du?' or 'Und Sie?'

ruleBlocks.title: Ask a name with 'wie'
ruleBlocks.content: Use 'Wie heißt du?' informally and 'Wie heißen Sie?' formally.

ruleBlocks.title: Ask origin with 'woher'
ruleBlocks.content: Use 'Woher kommst du?' or 'Woher kommen Sie?' to ask where someone comes from.

ruleBlocks.title: Ask residence with 'wo'
ruleBlocks.content: Use 'Wo wohnst du?' or 'Wo wohnen Sie?' to ask where someone lives.

ruleBlocks.title: Ask identity with 'wer'
ruleBlocks.content: Use 'Wer ist das?' when asking who a person is. The answer can begin with 'Das ist ...'.

sentenceStructure: Place the conjugated verb immediately after the question word.
Place the subject after the verb: 'Woher kommen Sie?'
Answer with a short statement and optionally return the question.

concepts: distinguish informal du from formal Sie
ask follow-up questions about family, work, and routines
clarify information when an answer is unclear
manage longer conversations with reasons and details

comparisons.summary: The identity lesson provides the answer content. This lesson supplies the questions that request each piece of information.
Question-word questions use the same conjugated verbs as statements, but the verb comes before the subject.

examples.de: A: Wie heißt du? B: Ich heiße Samir. Und du?
examples.en: A: What is your name? B: My name is Samir. And you?

examples.de: A: Woher kommen Sie? B: Ich komme aus Österreich.
examples.en: A: Where are you from? B: I come from Austria.

examples.de: A: Wo wohnst du? B: Ich wohne in Bremen.
examples.en: A: Where do you live? B: I live in Bremen.

examples.de: A: Wer ist das? B: Das ist Frau Neumann.
examples.en: A: Who is that? B: That is Ms Neumann.

examples.de: A: Guten Tag. Wie heißen Sie? B: Ich heiße Elena Rossi. A: Woher kommen Sie? B: Aus Italien.
examples.en: A: Good day. What is your name? B: My name is Elena Rossi. A: Where are you from? B: From Italy.

commonMistakes.reason: Use 'woher' to ask about origin or movement from a place.
In a direct question, the conjugated verb comes before the subject.
Formal 'Sie' requires the verb form ending in '-en'.
German asks someone's name with 'wie', not 'wer'.

specialCases: 'Woher?' can stand alone as a brief follow-up when the context is already clear.
Short answers such as 'Aus Spanien' are natural after a clear question even though they omit the full sentence.
'Wer sind Sie?' asks who someone is and can sound more direct than asking their name with 'Wie heißen Sie?'.
tips: Practice question and answer as one pair so word order becomes automatic.
Choose either du or Sie for an exchange and keep the pronoun and verb form consistent.
Use 'Und du?' or 'Und Sie?' to keep a conversation moving with very little language.

memoryHooks.title: Who, how, where, from where
memoryHooks.content: Wer asks who; wie asks the name; wo asks location; woher asks origin.

memoryHooks.title: Q-V-S
memoryHooks.content: For these questions, remember the order: question word, verb, subject.
